newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ denies studying ways out of Solid Energy.
newsitem.headline: NZ denies studying ways out of Solid Energy.

text.p: The New Zealand government on Monday rejected a newspaper report that it had appointed a New York-based team of investment bankers to advise it on ownership and funding options for Solid Energy, formerly Coal Corporation. "The government has not appointed New York bankers to investigate the ownership of Solid Energy, and Solid Energy is not on the list of assets which are currently under consideration for sale," a spokeswoman for State Owned Enterprises Minister Jenny Shipley said.
The only firms on that list at present are GPS (Government Property Services) and VTNZ (Vehicle Testing NZ), she added.

The Herald newspaper on Monday reported that analysts from an unidentified investment bank "will study sale options, (and) will also look at alternatives the government has for financing expansion of Solid Energy's operations".
Shipley's official said some U.S. bankers had been consulted about a proposal to build a NZ$130 million jetty on the West Coast of the South Island to export Solid Energy's coal.

The state miner, which has a net worth of NZ$115 million, was not one of the strategic assets excluded from sale by the December coalition agreement between nationalist New Zealand First and the conservative National Party.
In last Thursday's Budget Treasurer Winston Peters said sale of non-strategic assets would be considered on a case by case basis.

Shipley and Finance Minister Bill Birch said in a media release alongside the Budget that all state-owned enterprises would be asked to ensure they had the appropriate capital structure, including a debt to debt-plus-equity ratio at least as high as that of comparable private sector companies.
Political analysts have predicted this should return a stream of special dividends and capital repayments to the state.
